segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tested by the devil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterward he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the tester came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘A person will not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes out through the mouth of God.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written: ‘He will give his angels orders concerning you, and on their hands they will lift you up, so that you never strike your foot against a stone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Again it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go away, Satan! For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil left him, and look, angels came and waited on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And leaving Nazareth, he went and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah would be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations—

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light, and for those sitting in the land and shadow of death, a light has dawned.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Jesus began to proclaim and say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left their nets and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went around the whole of Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom and healing every disease and every ailment among the people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the report about him went out into all of Syria, and they brought to him all who were ill, gripped by various diseases and torments, those possessed by demons, those suffering seizures, and the paralyzed, and he healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And large crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.

notes.note: The Greek verb covers both testing someone to see what they are made of and enticing them to do wrong. In the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for Israel being tested in the wilderness, the story this passage echoes, and a related verb is rendered “put to the test” in verse 7. Most translations have “tempted”, which is not wrong, since the devil's aim is to make Jesus fail. “Tested” is used here to keep the link between verses 1, 3 and 7 visible.

All three of Jesus's replies quote Deuteronomy (8:3; 6:16; 6:13), from Moses's speech recalling Israel's forty years of testing in the wilderness. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have seen Jesus's forty days of hunger as a deliberate parallel to that story. The devil's quotation in verse 6 is from Psalm 91:11–12.

The Greek word means literally “little wing” and refers to a tip, edge or projecting part of a structure. Which part of the temple complex is meant is not known. Suggestions include a corner of the outer wall overlooking the Kidron valley and the roof edge of the sanctuary or of a colonnade. The traditional “pinnacle” is kept, but it should not be pictured as a spire.

The Greek says only that John was “handed over”, that is, delivered into custody. Most translations render it as “arrested” or “put in prison”, which is what happened. Matthew later uses this same verb repeatedly for Jesus being handed over to his death, so the literal wording is kept to let the parallel between John's fate and Jesus's be heard.

The “sea” is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long. Matthew follows Semitic usage in calling it a sea, where Luke calls it a lake. “Sea” is kept here because Matthew is linking Capernaum's location to the phrase “the way of the sea” in the Isaiah quotation that follows.

The quotation is from Isaiah 9:1–2. The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”, and in Jewish usage it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. Most translations use “Gentiles” here. “Nations” is the plainer equivalent and matches how the phrase is usually rendered in Isaiah itself.

“Repent” in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct, not only regret. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

Matthew's phrase has the plural “heavens”, a Semitic turn of phrase that most translations flatten to “heaven”. It means the same thing as “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels. The word for “kingdom” leans toward the activity of reigning more than a territory: the announcement is that God's rule has drawn near.
The Greek word refers to human beings in general, not males. The phrase plays on the brothers' trade: the same word is translated “fishermen” in verse 18.

“Gospel” has become a religious term and a name for a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “good news” and “gospel”.

The Greek word means literally “moonstruck”, reflecting the ancient belief that certain recurring attacks were governed by the moon. The one other New Testament use (Matthew 17:15) describes a boy who falls suddenly into fire and water, so seizures are evidently in view. Most modern translations say “epileptics”. The rendering here describes the symptoms without importing a modern diagnosis.

candidates.reason: It recurs across the Gospels, Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation, where translators split between “tempt” and “test”, and the choice (with the noun πειρασμός) affects the Lord's Prayer and James 1.
It ranges from bowing in homage before a human superior to worship of God, and varying between “worship”, “bow down” and “kneel before” across books would carry christological implications.
The same verb is used for John's arrest, Judas's act, Jesus's delivery to Pilate and God's giving up of the Son, and rendering it variously as “arrest”, “betray” and “deliver” hides the thread.
The plural is translated as either “Gentiles” or “nations” throughout the New Testament, and the choice needs a consistent policy, especially in Paul and Acts.
“Preach” now suggests a sermon in church, whereas the word means a herald's public announcement, so it needs one rendering across the Gospels, Acts and the letters.
